title: CHEM1A Practice Quiz — Objective 7: Atomic Structure & Periodicity (DRAFT pending Gilley approval)

items.stem: Calculate the frequency of light with wavelength 750 nm. (c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s)
items.explain: Convert first: 750 nm = 750 × 10⁻⁹ m. ν = c/λ = 4.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The 10⁵ answer skipped the nanometer-to-meter conversion — the unit's signature error, off by nine powers of ten.

items.stem: Which of these regions of the electromagnetic spectrum has the LONGEST wavelength?
items.explain: The spectrum runs radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-ray → gamma in order of shrinking wavelength (and climbing frequency and energy). Radio is the long-wavelength, low-energy end.

items.stem: Calculate the energy of one photon with frequency 2.00 × 10¹⁵ Hz. (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
items.explain: E = hν = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴)(2.00 × 10¹⁵) = 1.33 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. The 10⁴⁸ answer divided ν by h instead of multiplying; 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ forgot the frequency entirely.

items.stem: Dim blue light ejects electrons from a metal surface; extremely bright red light ejects none. This is because:
choices: Each photon's energy rides on its frequency, and ejection is a one-photon-per-electron event
Blue light contains more photons than red light
Red light is absorbed by the air before it arrives
Brightness has no physical effect on light
items.explain: The photoelectric effect's whole lesson: brightness sets the NUMBER of photons, frequency sets each photon's ENERGY. Each red photon arrives under the threshold no matter how many there are.

items.stem: Calculate the magnitude of the energy change when hydrogen's electron falls from n = 4 to n = 3. (R_H = 2.179 × 10⁻¹⁸ J)
items.explain: ΔE = R_H(1/9 − 1/16) = (2.179 × 10⁻¹⁸)(0.0486) = 1.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. The 1.82 answer used 1/3 − 1/4 instead of squaring the level numbers — the most common Bohr-equation slip.

items.stem: When a hydrogen atom ABSORBS a photon, its electron:
choices: Climbs to a higher level whose gap exactly matches the photon's energy
Falls to a lower level and speeds up
Leaves the atom, regardless of the photon's energy
Absorbs any photon and stores the extra energy for later
items.explain: Absorption climbs, emission falls, and the match must be exact — that exactness is why absorption spectra are sharp lines. There is no storing of partial energy between levels.

items.stem: Electrons show measurable wave behavior (λ = h/mv) but thrown baseballs do not, because:
choices: The baseball's mass makes its wavelength unimaginably small
Baseballs move too slowly to have a wavelength
The baseball's wavelength is too large to see
items.explain: Mass sits in the denominator: an electron's tiny mass gives an atom-sized wavelength; a baseball's gives roughly 10⁻³⁴ m. Charge is irrelevant to de Broglie's relation.

items.stem: The quantum-mechanical model replaced Bohr's circular orbits with orbitals because:
choices: Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly, so only probability regions can be drawn
Electrons were found to stand still inside atoms
Orbits were too difficult to calculate
Atoms were discovered to be flat
items.explain: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle forbids the exact-path picture; the orbital is the probability region that survives. Difficulty of calculation was never the issue.

items.stem: Which quantum number set is NOT allowed for any electron?
items.explain: mₗ runs only from −l to +l; with l = 1, mₗ = +2 is out of range. The other three sets are a 3d, a 2s, and a 4f electron respectively.

items.stem: The maximum number of electrons in any d subshell is:
items.explain: A d subshell (l = 2) holds five orbitals × two electrons = 10. Six is the p count, fourteen the f count, two a single orbital's limit (Pauli).

items.stem: The ground-state electron configuration of magnesium (Z = 12) is:
items.explain: Twelve electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² = [Ne] 3s². The 3s¹ 3p¹ version is an EXCITED state — ground state fills lowest-energy first (Aufbau). [Ar] already contains 18 electrons, too many.

items.stem: The ground-state electron configuration of the Al³⁺ ion (Z = 13) is:
items.explain: Count first: 13 − 3 = 10 electrons → the neon configuration. The second choice forgot to remove any electrons; the third ADDED three instead of removing.

items.stem: Tin (Sn) sits in group 14 (4A). How many valence electrons does it have?
items.explain: Main-group number reads off the valence count: group 14 → ns² np² → 4 valence electrons. Fourteen reads the group label as a count; fifty is all of tin's electrons.

items.stem: An element's configuration ends in 4s² 4p². This element is in:
items.explain: n = 4 on the valence shell puts it in period 4; s² p² is four valence electrons, group 14. The table position and the configuration are the same information written two ways.

items.stem: Which atom is the SMALLEST: nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine?
choices: They are the same size — same shell
items.explain: Same shell, but effective nuclear charge climbs across the period: nine protons pull the n = 2 shell tighter than seven. Same-shell-same-size is exactly the misconception the Zeff story replaces.

items.stem: An element's second ionization energy is enormously larger than its first, while its first is quite low. The element is most likely in group:
choices: 1 — one easy valence electron, then a noble-gas core
items.explain: The giant jump marks the wall where valence electrons run out and the core begins. One cheap electron, then the wall → exactly one valence electron → group 1.

items.stem: ELECTRON AFFINITY is best described as:
choices: The energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron — for many nonmetals, energy is released
The energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom
An atom's pull on the electrons it shares within a chemical bond
The number of extra electrons an atom is able to accept
items.explain: Electron affinity is the energy change of GAINING an electron: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g) — and for many nonmetals that change releases energy. 'Energy required to remove' is ionization energy, the reverse process; the shared-electron pull is electronegativity, which lives inside bonds and has no energy units; a simple count of acceptable electrons is neither quantity.

items.stem: An atom is in its GROUND STATE when:
choices: Its electrons occupy the lowest-energy arrangement available
It has lost all its electrons
items.explain: Ground state = lowest-energy electron arrangement — the configuration the Aufbau order builds. Electrons never stop moving, and temperature is a different variable entirely.

choices: Inner electrons canceling part of the nuclear pull felt by outer electrons
The nucleus protecting itself from radiation
Electrons repelling photons away from the atom
The outermost shell blocking chemical reactions
items.explain: Core electrons sit between the nucleus and the valence shell, canceling part of the pull — the difference between Z and Zeff. It is an electron-electron effect, nothing to do with radiation.
